system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Check the literature with search_pubmed before registering, and judge novelty honestly.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 30 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Mission: Search for synthetic-lethal paralog dependencies: genes whose loss (LOSS_ or MUT_ biomarkers) makes cells depend on a paralog or functional backup.

Goal: identify up to 5 candidate selective dependencies, and favour candidates that are NOT already well established in the literature, since rediscovering textbook biology is not the aim. Pre-register, replicate, and submit honest findings, including failures.

content.thinking:
I'm weighing a first hypothesis: that losing ATP6V0E2 could be compensated by its paralog ATP6V0E1, since both are V-ATPase c-subunit isoforms, with E2 being more tissue-restricted and E1 essential. Literature searches turned up nothing on this, which makes it look novel. I'm now wondering whether the same effect would show up outside lymphoid lineages, and I'm starting to check that within esophagus and head-and-neck samples.

I'm lining up the remaining candidate pairs: ATP6V0A1 to ATP6V0A2 looks lymphoid-heavy with at least one computational paper nearby, DMXL2 to DMXL1 has existing V-ATPase literature, and RPP25 to RPP25L is already established. I'm leaning toward H1 and H2, maybe H3, and I plan to register all three before running replications.

input.mechanism: ATP6V0E1 and ATP6V0E2 are paralogous c-ring/proteolipid subunits of the V-ATPase V0 domain. Cells that lost ATP6V0E2 expression rely on ATP6V0E1 for lysosomal/endosomal proton pumping; ATP6V0E1 loss is therefore selectively lethal in ATP6V0E2-low cells (paralog buffering).

ATP6V0A1 (a1) and ATP6V0A2 (a2) are paralogous V0-a subunit isoforms governing V-ATPase localization. Loss of a1 expression makes cells depend on a2 for V-ATPase function, which is a paralog buffering synthetic lethality.

DMXL1 and DMXL2 are paralogous WD40/rabconnectin-3 components of the rabconnectin-3 complex that regulates V-ATPase assembly and endosomal acidification. DMXL2 loss may make cells depend on DMXL1 for V-ATPase function.

content.thinking: The H3 result replicated, though the Sanger sample has only three altered lines, so it's a weak signal that still meets the stated criteria. H2 didn't replicate, since Sanger had no altered lines. With two budget units left, I'm going to stop here, and I'm considering whether to look further into DMXL2 in the literature before submitting. On novelty, H1 wasn't found in the literature, while H3 and H2 are partly known, H3 through the DMXL1 V-ATPase link. I'll submit with honest caveats.

findings.claim: Lines with LOSS of ATP6V0E2 (V0 proton-pump c-ring paralog) depend strongly on ATP6V0E1; held-out Broad beta -0.90 (p=1e-29, 18 altered) and Sanger beta -0.88 (p=8e-26, 11 altered). Discovery effect was not confined to one lineage (esophagus/stomach and head-and-neck within-lineage effects both ~-0.9), though ATP6V0E1 is a V-ATPase core subunit and the 'other lines' mean effect is -0.2, so the therapeutic window needs checking.

LOSS of ATP6V0A1 predicted dependence on ATP6V0A2 in discovery (t=-15.8) and held-out Broad lines (beta -0.65, p=3e-12, only 4 altered lines), but the discovery signal was dominated by lymphoid/B-cell and prostate/myeloid lines, and Sanger had zero altered lines so the test could not be run. Not confirmed as a general selective dependency.

LOSS of DMXL2 predicts dependence on DMXL1 (held-out Broad beta -0.57, p=8e-15; Sanger beta -0.58, p=2e-9), consistent with rabconnectin-3 paralog buffering of V-ATPase regulation. Caveats: lymphoid/myeloid-enriched in discovery, and only 3 altered lines in Sanger, so the replication is statistically weak.

input.summary: I surveyed LOSS_/MUT_ biomarker→dependency pairs and prioritized paralog-type pairs. Three hypotheses were pre-registered and tested. H1 (LOSS_ATP6V0E2 → ATP6V0E1) replicated in both held-out Broad and independent Sanger screens and has no literature hits, making it the strongest novel candidate. H3 (LOSS_DMXL2 → DMXL1) also replicated, though with few Sanger altered lines and partial prior literature on DMXL1–V-ATPase. H2 (LOSS_ATP6V0A1 → ATP6V0A2) did not replicate: its Sanger test was impossible because no lines carried the loss, and the discovery signal was driven largely by lymphoid lines. Caveats: the V-ATPase targets are broadly important, so selectivity windows are uncertain. I did not test RPP25→RPP25L, which has a published paralog-interaction study (PMID 35417719), so it is not novel. Two replication calls remain unused.
